newsitem.title: USA: SEC proposals would ease investing by localities.
newsitem.headline: SEC proposals would ease investing by localities.

text.p: The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission voted on Wednesday to propose rules that would affect investing by state and local governments.
The draft rules would exempt private funds that consist solely of "highly sophisticated investors" from SEC rules governing investment companies, the SEC said.
Such investors would include individuals who hold $5 million in investments, as well as institutions with $25 million in investments, including states and localities.

The draft rules would implement those provisions of the National Securities Markets Improvement Act of 1996 -- passed by Congress in September and signed by President Clinton on October 11 -- that affect private investment companies.
The law directs the SEC to adopt rules exempting private investment companies with only sophisticated investors from the provisions of the Investment Company Act of 1940 by April 9, 1997.
The 1940 law required for the first time that the SEC register and regulate investment companies.
The SEC was required to regulate how funds price, allocate and promote securities in their portfolios, for example.
SEC Commissioner Isaac Hunt expressed concern at today's meeting that the new proposal would exempt many city pension funds and other less sophisticated municipal investors from 1940 Act regulation.

Barry Barbash, director of SEC's investment management division, said: "It would not be unreasonable to predict that sometime down the road some...sophisticated participant would be in a pool that liquidates, blows up.

"(But) I am not sure that says (there is) anything wrong with this particular provision. There are always going to be aberrations and there are always going to be deals that don't work. You see that now and we're sure you'll see that in the future."
A Hunt aide said: "We will monitor the situation. (But) Congress has enacted this legislation with these parameters, and it is our responsibility to implement this to the best of our ability."
